input.question: Our energy sector CII organization has an asset inventory spreadsheet updated quarterly by the IT team. The inventory covers enterprise servers, network devices, and workstations. The SCADA historian servers and PLCs in the OT network are tracked separately in an Excel file maintained by the OT team, but this file has not been reconciled with the IT inventory for the past 18 months. Our cybersecurity policy states that a unified asset inventory covering all CII assets must be maintained and reviewed monthly. Identify the compliance gaps in this situation.

ground_truth.expected_response: There are multiple compliance gaps here. First, the unified asset inventory required by CCoP 2.0 Section 4.1 (Identification: asset management) is not being maintained — the IT and OT inventories are siloed and have not been reconciled for 18 months, meaning the organization does not have an accurate picture of its CII asset base. Second, the quarterly review cadence for the IT inventory and the 18-month stale OT inventory both violate the organization's own policy requiring monthly review — this is a policy-vs-practice gap that auditors will note immediately. Third, the OT assets (SCADA historian, PLCs) are CII components that fall within the mandatory scope of the asset inventory requirement under the OT Addendum; maintaining them in an unreconciled shadow spreadsheet creates risks of unmanaged assets. The practical risks include unpatched OT assets going undetected, unauthorized additions to the OT network outside audit scope, and inability to provide accurate CII boundary documentation to CSA. To close these gaps: establish a single consolidated inventory process with monthly reconciliation between IT and OT teams, assign ownership of the unified inventory to a named role, and implement automated discovery tooling appropriate for the OT environment.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 4.1 requires CIIOs to maintain a comprehensive and current inventory of all CII assets within the digital boundary
OT assets (SCADA, PLCs) are within the CII digital boundary and must be included in the mandatory asset inventory
An 18-month gap in reconciliation of the OT inventory means the asset register does not reflect the current state of CII systems
A policy-practice gap exists when the organization's own policy requires monthly review but actual practice is quarterly (IT) or effectively annual (OT)
Unreconciled IT and OT asset inventories prevent accurate digital boundary documentation required for CSA audit

reasoning_chain: Identify that the organization has siloed IT and OT asset inventories not reconciled for 18 months
Map this against CCoP 2.0 Section 4.1 requirement for a comprehensive, current asset inventory
Identify that OT assets (SCADA historian, PLCs) are within CII scope and must be included
Note the policy-practice gap: policy requires monthly review; actual cadence is quarterly (IT) and effectively lapsed (OT)
Identify that the lack of a unified inventory creates audit evidence weakness for CII boundary documentation
Characterize the gaps as: (1) incomplete coverage, (2) stale data, (3) policy-practice inconsistency, (4) missing OT scope
acceptable_variations: May reference specific OT Addendum clauses on OT asset management
May recommend automated OT discovery tools (passive scanning to avoid disrupting ICS)
May note that the inventory gap also affects vulnerability management and patch management processes downstream

forbidden_claims: Separate IT and OT inventories satisfy CCoP requirements if both exist
Quarterly review is sufficient for CII asset management
hallucination_patterns: Citing non-existent CCoP clause numbers
Attributing specific update frequency requirements that CCoP does not specify

input.question: A water utility CII organization conducts an annual cybersecurity risk assessment as required by CCoP 2.0. The last completed risk assessment is dated 14 months ago. The CISO explains that the team is currently conducting this year's risk assessment and expects to complete it within the next 6 weeks. The risk register maintained from the previous assessment has not been updated to reflect two significant changes: (1) three new SCADA remote telemetry units (RTUs) were added to the OT network 4 months ago, and (2) a new third-party water quality monitoring vendor was given remote access 3 months ago. Is there a compliance gap? If so, identify it precisely.

ground_truth.expected_response: Yes, there are at least two compliance gaps. First, the risk assessment cycle gap: while an annual risk assessment being 14 months old with an in-progress replacement may be defensible if the timeline is genuinely uncontrollable, the gap itself represents a lapse in meeting the annual risk assessment cadence required under CCoP 2.0 Section 4.2. CSA auditors will scrutinize the completion date and the reason for the 2-month overrun. Second, and more critically, a material gap exists because the risk register was not updated to reflect two significant changes to the CII environment: three new RTUs added to the OT network and a new remote-access vendor. CCoP 2.0 requires that risk assessments be updated when there are significant changes to the CII system — adding OT devices and granting third-party remote access both qualify as significant changes triggering an update obligation. Third, the new vendor's remote access represents an unassessed supply chain risk: CCoP 2.0 requires vendor risk assessments before granting access to CII systems. The risk register currently shows no assessed risks for this vendor. The gaps are: (1) overdue annual risk assessment, (2) risk register not updated for significant system changes, (3) third-party vendor access granted without documented risk assessment.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 4.2 requires annual cybersecurity risk assessments for CII systems
Risk assessments must be updated when significant changes occur to the CII system, such as new OT devices or new third-party access
CCoP 2.0 requires vendor risk assessments before granting third-party access to CII systems
Adding RTUs to the OT network and granting new remote vendor access both constitute significant changes requiring risk assessment updates
A risk register that does not reflect the current CII environment cannot serve as accurate audit evidence

reasoning_chain: Identify the annual risk assessment cadence requirement and note the 14-month gap
Assess whether the in-progress assessment mitigates the lapse — it reduces but does not eliminate the gap
Identify the two significant system changes (RTUs, vendor access) that should have triggered risk assessment updates
Map vendor remote access against supply chain risk assessment requirement
Characterize gaps: overdue assessment, unupdated risk register, vendor access without documented risk assessment
Note that all three gaps would be visible to a CSA auditor reviewing the risk register and audit log
acceptable_variations: May distinguish between the annual cadence gap (process lapse) and the material change gaps (higher severity)
May recommend interim risk assessment or addendum covering the new RTUs and vendor
May note that vendor remote access may also implicate access control requirements under Section 5

forbidden_claims: An in-progress risk assessment remedies the compliance gap for past periods
Adding OT devices does not require risk register updates if an annual assessment is pending
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific clause numbers for vendor assessment timelines that CCoP does not specify
Attributing specific RTU security configuration requirements not in CCoP

input.question: A banking sector CII organization's cybersecurity policy states that multi-factor authentication (MFA) is mandatory for all privileged access to CII systems. In practice, the implementation is as follows: (a) MFA is enforced for all external remote access via the VPN gateway, (b) MFA is enforced for Active Directory domain admin accounts, (c) Local admin accounts on CII servers do not require MFA because they can only be used when physically at the server console, (d) Service accounts used for automated processes between CII systems are excluded from MFA as they cannot support interactive authentication. Identify the policy-vs-practice gaps and any compliance gaps against CCoP 2.0.

ground_truth.expected_response: There are both policy-vs-practice gaps and CCoP compliance gaps here. The policy-vs-practice gap: the organization's own policy mandates MFA for all privileged access, but the implementation excludes local admin accounts and service accounts. This divergence between stated policy and actual practice is itself a compliance gap that auditors will identify when they compare the policy document against the access control configuration. Regarding the local admin account exception: this is partially defensible — requiring physical presence at the server console is a compensating control that reduces remote exploitation risk. However, the exception is not documented as a formal exception with risk acceptance, which is required under CCoP governance requirements. Physical access controls to the server room must be documented to support this compensating control. Regarding the service account exception: this is a more significant gap. CCoP 2.0 requires that privileged service accounts be managed through a privileged access management (PAM) process including rotation, least privilege, and access logging. Excluding service accounts entirely from the MFA policy without a documented risk acceptance and compensating controls is non-compliant. Service accounts are a common lateral movement vector — they represent elevated risk, not reduced risk. The gaps are: (1) policy-practice inconsistency requiring formal exception documentation, (2) undocumented local admin exception, (3) service accounts lacking PAM controls, (4) missing formal risk acceptance for both exceptions.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 5.3.1 requires MFA for privileged access to CII systems
Service accounts with privileged access to CII systems require PAM controls including rotation, least privilege, and access logging
Exceptions to mandatory security controls require formal risk acceptance documentation and compensating controls
A policy-practice gap exists when the written policy mandates a control that the actual configuration does not enforce
Physical console access as a compensating control for MFA can be defensible if documented with physical access controls evidenced

reasoning_chain: Compare the policy statement ('MFA mandatory for all privileged access') against the four implementation points
Identify that local admin and service account exclusions create a policy-practice gap
Assess the local admin console exception against CCoP requirements — partial compensating control, missing documentation
Assess the service account exclusion — this is a higher-severity gap as service accounts are privileged and require PAM controls
Determine that both exceptions require formal risk acceptance documentation under CCoP governance requirements
Characterize the gap set: policy-practice inconsistency, undocumented exceptions, service account PAM gap
acceptable_variations: May recommend PAM tooling for service account management
May note that console-only local admin accounts are lower risk but still require exception documentation
May reference Active Directory tiering model as best practice for the local admin scenario

forbidden_claims: Service accounts are not subject to MFA requirements because they cannot support interactive authentication
Physical console restriction fully satisfies MFA requirements for local admin accounts without documentation
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific PAM product requirements from CCoP
Attributing specific service account rotation intervals that CCoP does not mandate

input.question: A healthcare CII organization has completed its annual cybersecurity awareness training programme. The training was delivered online to all staff and completion records show 94% completion. The CISO presents this to the board as evidence of compliance with CCoP 2.0 training requirements. Upon reviewing the records, the Risk Manager notes: (1) clinical staff (nurses, doctors) completed a general cybersecurity awareness module but no role-specific training relevant to handling patient data systems or medical device security, (2) the CISO and 3 senior IT managers received the same general awareness module as all staff, (3) no training records exist for 3 contract OT engineers who maintain the hospital's building management and medical device networks, (4) board members received no training. Identify all compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: Multiple compliance gaps exist in this training programme. First, CCoP 2.0 requires role-based cybersecurity training, not just general awareness. Clinical staff handling patient data systems require training specific to their role, including data handling, phishing awareness in clinical contexts, and medical device security basics. Providing the same general module does not satisfy the role-based requirement. Second, cybersecurity leadership (CISO, senior IT managers) must receive training appropriate to their roles — technical leadership training that goes beyond general awareness to include threat landscape, incident command, and regulatory obligations. Third, the contract OT engineers maintaining medical device and building management networks have no training records. CCoP 2.0 requires that all personnel with access to CII — including contractors — complete appropriate cybersecurity training. The 6% non-completion gap and absent contractor training are audit findings. Fourth, board members must receive training to meet CCoP 2.0 governance requirements for BoD cybersecurity knowledge and awareness — the absence of any board training is a governance compliance gap. The summary of gaps: (1) training is general, not role-based; (2) leadership training is insufficient; (3) contractors excluded; (4) board not trained; (5) 6% non-completion with no remediation plan.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 requires role-based cybersecurity training for all personnel with access to CII, not just general awareness
Board of Directors must receive cybersecurity training to meet CCoP governance requirements
Contractors and third-party personnel with access to CII systems are subject to the same training requirements as employees
Role-based training must be appropriate to the individual's role — clinical staff, leadership, OT engineers each require different content
94% completion without a documented remediation plan for the 6% non-completion is an incomplete training programme

reasoning_chain: Assess the training programme against CCoP role-based training requirements
Identify that general awareness modules do not satisfy role-based training for clinical staff, leadership, or OT personnel
Map contractor exclusion against CCoP requirement for all CII-access personnel
Identify the board training gap as a governance compliance issue
Count and characterize each gap: (1) role-based gap for clinical staff, (2) leadership training gap, (3) contractor exclusion, (4) board training gap, (5) non-completion without remediation
acceptable_variations: May specify what role-appropriate content for clinical staff should include
May reference the upcoming 2026 regulatory requirement for formal board cybersecurity training
May recommend a training matrix mapping roles to required training modules

forbidden_claims: 94% completion of general awareness training satisfies CCoP training requirements
Board training is voluntary under CCoP 2.0
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific training hour requirements that CCoP does not mandate
Attributing specific clinical staff training content requirements from non-CCoP frameworks

input.question: A transport sector CII organization operates a rail signalling system. The network architecture has the following characteristics: the corporate IT network connects to the internet; a DMZ separates the corporate network from the operational network; the signalling system runs on a dedicated network connected to the operational network via a router with firewall rules. The Risk Manager reviews the patch management records and finds: (a) enterprise systems (corporate network) are patched monthly following the standard vulnerability management process; (b) the signalling system's embedded controllers have not received firmware updates in 3 years because the vendor requires a 4-hour maintenance window that the operations team has not been able to schedule; (c) a vendor support contract for the signalling system expired 8 months ago and has not been renewed. Identify the compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: There are three interconnected compliance gaps here. First, the 3-year firmware update gap on the signalling system's embedded controllers constitutes a patch management compliance gap under CCoP 2.0 Section 5.5 (patch management). CCoP requires that CII systems receive security patches within defined timeframes based on vulnerability criticality. A 3-year gap is not defensible as 'awaiting a maintenance window' — the organization is required to implement a patch management process that includes planning for OT maintenance windows. The operational constraint is real but must be addressed through formal risk treatment: scheduling the maintenance window, requesting a waiver if patching is genuinely infeasible, or implementing compensating controls (additional network monitoring, enhanced access controls). Second, the expired vendor support contract means the organization has no access to security patches, vulnerability notifications, or incident response support for the signalling system — a critical CII component. CCoP requires that support arrangements for CII systems remain current. Third, together these gaps mean the organization cannot demonstrate an effective patch management process for a critical OT component — this would be a significant audit finding. A waiver request for the 4-hour maintenance window constraint may be appropriate, but must be accompanied by compensating controls and a credible remediation timeline.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 5.5 requires a patch management process covering all CII systems including OT components
A 3-year absence of firmware updates on CII OT systems is a material patch management compliance gap
Expired vendor support contracts for CII systems compromise the ability to receive patches and security updates, creating a compliance risk
Operational constraints on patching OT systems require formal risk treatment: waiver request, compensating controls, or scheduled maintenance windows
The waiver process under Section 11(7) is available for operationally infeasible patching requirements but requires compensating controls

reasoning_chain: Identify the 3-year firmware gap on OT systems against CCoP patch management requirements
Assess whether 'cannot schedule maintenance window' is an adequate justification — it is not; it requires formal risk treatment
Identify the expired vendor support contract as a secondary gap blocking future patching capability
Connect these gaps: without active support, future patching becomes impossible
Characterize the combined gap as an OT patch management programme failure requiring immediate action
Identify waiver as a potential pathway if patching is genuinely infeasible within operational constraints
acceptable_variations: May recommend compensating controls during the period of unpatched systems (enhanced monitoring, network access restrictions)
May identify the vendor support expiry as triggering a technology refresh decision
May note that the DMZ architecture partially mitigates but does not eliminate the vulnerability exposure

forbidden_claims: Operational constraints exempt CII OT systems from patch management requirements
An expired vendor support contract does not create a compliance gap if the system is functioning normally
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific patch window timelines from CCoP that are not specified
Attributing patching requirements from NIST or IEC 62443 as CCoP mandates

input.question: A government sector CII organization's cybersecurity policy states that all vendor access to CII systems must be conducted on-site under supervision of an internal staff member. The Risk Manager reviews the vendor access log for the past 6 months and finds: (a) 12 vendor maintenance sessions were conducted on-site as required; (b) 4 sessions were conducted remotely by the SCADA vendor following a software update — the IT manager approved these by email citing 'operational urgency'; (c) 1 session involved the vendor accessing the system via a personal laptop because the dedicated jump server was under maintenance. Identify all compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: Three compliance gaps exist in this vendor access record. First, the 4 remote vendor sessions violate both organizational policy and CCoP 2.0 supply chain requirements. CCoP 2.0 requires that vendor access to CII systems be performed on-site. Remote access by vendors, even in cases of operational urgency, does not satisfy this requirement. The IT manager's email approval is not a valid exception mechanism — deviations from this requirement require formal waiver or documented risk acceptance at the appropriate governance level, not ad-hoc approval. Second, the 'operational urgency' justification is a pattern risk: if IT managers can approve remote vendor access ad-hoc, the policy exception is being routinely normalized, undermining the control. This is a governance gap in the exception management process. Third, the session where the vendor used a personal laptop is a significant security control violation: CCoP requires that devices connecting to CII use approved, hardened, organization-managed or formally vetted equipment. A vendor's personal laptop does not meet this standard — it could be compromised, may not have security software, and may exfiltrate data without detection. This is also a policy violation (on-site access procedure should specify use of organization-provided or approved equipment). The gaps are: (1) remote access violating on-site policy and CCoP requirements, (2) ad-hoc exception approvals without governance process, (3) unvetted personal device used on CII system.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 requires that all vendor access to CII systems be conducted on-site
Vendor devices connecting to CII must be approved and meet security standards — personal laptops are not acceptable
Ad-hoc email approvals from IT managers do not constitute valid policy exceptions — formal exception management requires governance-level approval
Repeated ad-hoc exceptions to a security control indicate a governance gap in the exception management process
'Operational urgency' is not listed as a valid ground for bypassing on-site vendor access requirements in CCoP

reasoning_chain: Review the vendor access log against the on-site requirement in both policy and CCoP
Identify the 4 remote sessions as policy violations and potential CCoP non-compliance
Assess the IT manager email approval mechanism — not a valid exception process
Identify the personal laptop session as a device security violation compounding the policy breach
Characterize the gaps: (1) remote access violation, (2) exception governance gap, (3) device security violation
Note that the remote sessions during software updates are higher risk — software update sessions carry supply chain attack risk
acceptable_variations: May recommend implementing a formal vendor access exception request process
May note that jump server unavailability should have caused postponement, not workaround
May recommend a dedicated air-gapped vendor access terminal as a compensating control

forbidden_claims: Email approval from IT management is sufficient authorization for remote vendor access to CII
Operational urgency is a valid ground for remote vendor access under CCoP
hallucination_patterns: Citing a specific maximum session time for vendor access that CCoP does not specify
Attributing NIST SP 800-171 supply chain requirements as CCoP mandates

input.question: A maritime port CII organization's cybersecurity policy states that a vulnerability assessment (VA) must be conducted every 6 months and a penetration test (PT) must be conducted annually. The last VA was conducted 11 months ago. The last PT was conducted 22 months ago. The CISO explains that the VA vendor contract lapsed and procurement of a new vendor took time; the PT delay was due to the operations team being unable to schedule a test window that would not disrupt port operations. The organization also completed a major network segmentation project 4 months ago, adding new DMZ zones for the vessel traffic management system. Identify the compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: Multiple compliance gaps are present. First, the VA gap: the last VA was 11 months ago against a 6-month requirement — the organization is 5 months overdue. The vendor contract lapse is an operational explanation, not a compliance justification. The 6-month VA cadence in CCoP 2.0 Section 5.6 is a mandatory requirement; procurement delays must be managed to maintain compliance. This is a current, active compliance gap requiring immediate action. Second, the PT gap: at 22 months against an annual requirement, the organization is 10 months overdue. Operational scheduling constraints are a recognized challenge for OT environments, but they do not suspend CCoP obligations. A waiver request may be available if genuine operational infeasibility can be demonstrated, but no such waiver was sought. Third, and most critically, the major network segmentation project 4 months ago introduced significant changes to the CII architecture (new DMZ zones for the vessel traffic management system). CCoP requires that significant changes to CII architecture trigger a targeted VA/PT of the affected components. No VA or PT was conducted following the segmentation project — meaning the new architecture has never been independently tested. This is a gap of higher severity than the cadence gaps alone. The gaps are: (1) VA overdue by 5 months, (2) PT overdue by 10 months, (3) no post-change VA/PT following major architecture change.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 5.6 requires vulnerability assessments every 6 months for CII systems
CCoP 2.0 requires penetration testing on an annual basis for CII systems
Significant architectural changes to CII systems trigger a requirement for targeted VA/PT of the affected components
Vendor procurement delays and operational scheduling constraints do not suspend CCoP compliance obligations
No VA or PT was conducted following the network segmentation project — new attack surface from DMZ changes is untested

reasoning_chain: Identify the VA cadence gap: 11 months against 6-month requirement = 5 months overdue
Identify the PT cadence gap: 22 months against annual requirement = 10 months overdue
Note that the major network segmentation project introduces a third, higher-priority gap: no post-change testing
Map the post-change testing requirement to CCoP Section 5.6 provisions on significant changes
Rank the gaps by severity: post-change untested architecture > overdue PT > overdue VA
Note that waiver process was not utilized despite operational constraints — this is also an oversight
acceptable_variations: May recommend emergency VA of the new DMZ architecture as an immediate priority
May recommend scoped PT of the vessel traffic management system DMZ specifically
May note that the network segmentation project itself represents a positive security improvement

forbidden_claims: Annual PT cadence means PT can be delayed to align with operational windows without a compliance gap
No VA is required following architecture changes if the annual VA is upcoming
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific VA scope requirements from CREST or OWASP as CCoP mandates
Attributing specific penetration testing methodology requirements CCoP does not specify

input.question: A telecoms CII organization documents in its cybersecurity policy that an incident response plan (IRP) exists, has been tested in the past 12 months, and is reviewed annually. The Risk Manager discovers the following: the IRP was created 2 years ago and states it will be reviewed annually. However, the last documented review was 18 months ago. A tabletop exercise was conducted 14 months ago but the after-action report (AAR) identified 5 improvement actions; only 2 of these have been completed. No full-scale exercise involving external parties (CSA, sector partners) has been conducted. Is there a compliance gap, and if so, identify all gaps precisely.

ground_truth.expected_response: Yes, there are compliance gaps across both the IRP maintenance and exercise dimensions. First, IRP review cadence: the policy states annual review but the last review was 18 months ago — a 6-month overdue gap. The IRP document itself acknowledges the annual review requirement, making this a clear policy-practice gap. Second, the exercise improvement actions: the tabletop AAR identified 5 improvement actions and only 2 have been completed. CCoP 2.0 requires that exercise findings be tracked to closure. Leaving 3 improvement actions open 14 months after the exercise represents a failure to maintain an effective incident response capability and would be visible in any audit. Third, CCoP 2.0 requires that cybersecurity exercises include relevant external parties, including participation in national exercises or engagement with CSA. No such exercise has been conducted. This is a gap in the exercise programme design, not just cadence. The policy also overstates compliance: it claims the IRP has been tested in the past 12 months (the tabletop was 14 months ago) — this creates an audit accuracy risk if the policy document is presented as evidence. The gaps are: (1) IRP review overdue by 6 months, (2) exercise improvement actions not tracked to closure, (3) no external-party exercise, (4) policy overstates compliance status.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 requires that the incident response plan be reviewed and updated at defined intervals, typically at least annually
Exercise findings and improvement actions must be tracked to closure — open actions represent unaddressed IRP weaknesses
CCoP 2.0 requires cybersecurity exercises involving external parties and participation in national or sector exercises
A policy document that overstates compliance (claims recent testing when testing is overdue) creates audit accuracy risk
The IRP review gap is also a policy-practice gap because the IRP itself states the annual review requirement

reasoning_chain: Compare IRP review date (18 months ago) against annual review requirement
Identify the policy-practice gap: the IRP document states annual review, but review is 6 months overdue
Review the exercise AAR: 3/5 improvement actions remain open 14 months later
Map open improvement actions against requirement to track findings to closure
Identify the absence of external-party exercises as a design gap in the exercise programme
Note the policy inaccuracy: policy claims testing within 12 months when tabletop was 14 months ago
acceptable_variations: May recommend specific types of exercises to include external parties (CSA, sector partners)
May suggest a structured exercise improvement action tracking process
May distinguish tabletop exercises from full-scale exercises and their different value

forbidden_claims: A tabletop exercise with internal staff satisfies all CCoP exercise requirements
Open exercise improvement actions are acceptable if some actions have been completed
hallucination_patterns: Citing a specific number of required exercises per year that CCoP does not mandate
Attributing NIST SP 800-61 incident response requirements as CCoP mandates

input.question: A banking CII organization documents that it conducts cybersecurity threat modelling as part of its risk assessment programme. The Risk Manager reviews the threat modelling artefacts and finds: (a) a threat model was created 2 years ago using a STRIDE-based approach; (b) the threat model covers the core banking application and its network connections; (c) three new microservices were added to the CII architecture 8 months ago to support open banking APIs — these are not in the threat model; (d) the threat model has never been reviewed by an independent party; (e) the threat actors list in the model was last reviewed 2 years ago and does not reflect current threat intelligence about ransomware targeting financial sector CII. What compliance gaps exist?

ground_truth.expected_response: The threat modelling programme has gaps across coverage, currency, and independence dimensions. First, coverage gap: the three new microservices supporting open banking APIs were added 8 months ago and are absent from the threat model. Open banking APIs introduce external-facing attack surface, third-party data flows, and new trust boundaries — all of which require threat modelling. A threat model that does not reflect the current CII architecture is not fit for its CCoP compliance purpose. Second, currency gap: the threat model's threat actor list is 2 years old and does not incorporate current threat intelligence on ransomware targeting financial CII. CCoP 2.0 requires threat models to be updated based on new threat intelligence, particularly for high-value CII like banking. An outdated threat actor profile leads to incorrectly prioritized controls. Third, independence: CCoP 2.0 and its supporting guide (CSA's Guide to Cyber Threat Modelling) require that threat models be reviewed by suitably qualified independent parties — the threat model has never been independently reviewed. Fourth, the combination of these gaps means the threat model cannot serve as reliable evidence in a CCoP audit. The risk register derived from an incomplete, outdated threat model may also be unreliable. Gaps: (1) coverage gap for new API microservices, (2) outdated threat intelligence/actor list, (3) no independent review, (4) derivative risk register reliability risk.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 requires cyber threat modelling as part of the risk assessment methodology for CII systems
Threat models must be updated when significant changes are made to the CII architecture, such as adding new microservices or API endpoints
CSA's Guide to Cyber Threat Modelling requires that threat models be reviewed by suitably qualified independent parties
key_facts.source: CSA Guide to Cyber Threat Modelling

key_facts.fact: Threat actor profiles and threat intelligence inputs to threat models must be kept current to maintain relevance
A threat model that does not cover the current CII architecture cannot support an accurate risk register

reasoning_chain: Assess threat model coverage against current CII architecture — identify the 3 microservices gap
Assess threat model currency — identify that the threat actor list predates current ransomware threat landscape
Identify the absence of independent review as a process gap
Connect threat model gaps to downstream risk register reliability
Characterize gaps: (1) coverage, (2) currency, (3) independence, (4) derivative risk register impact
acceptable_variations: May recommend specific threat modelling approaches suitable for microservices/API architectures
May recommend integration of threat intelligence feeds into the threat modelling update process
May note that open banking API threat models should include data flow analysis across third-party integrations

forbidden_claims: A 2-year-old threat model is acceptable if no major architecture changes occurred
Independent review of threat models is optional under CCoP
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific threat modelling methodology requirements (STRIDE, PASTA) as CCoP mandates
Attributing MITRE ATT&CK framework requirements as CCoP mandates

input.question: An aviation CII organization has a cybersecurity policy that states all CII system changes must go through a change management process that includes a cybersecurity impact assessment (CIA). The Risk Manager reviews recent change records and finds: (a) 45 changes in the last quarter went through the formal change management process with documented CIAs; (b) 3 emergency changes to the air traffic control system were applied directly by the vendor technician following approval from the operations director — no CIA was conducted and no formal change record was created until 2 weeks after the changes; (c) the CIA template used for the 45 formal changes does not include questions about OT-specific risks (e.g., impact on control system availability, protocol changes). Are there compliance gaps?

ground_truth.expected_response: Yes, there are two categories of compliance gaps here. First, the emergency change exceptions: the 3 emergency changes to the air traffic control system bypassed the CIA requirement and were not formally recorded until 2 weeks after the fact. CCoP 2.0 requires that all changes to CII systems undergo a change management process — emergency changes may have an expedited path, but they cannot bypass the CIA entirely. An after-the-fact record 2 weeks later does not constitute a CIA; it is a retrospective documentation exercise. The operations director approval does not substitute for a cybersecurity impact assessment. This is a policy-practice gap where the emergency change process lacks cybersecurity controls. Second, the CIA template gap: the template used for formal changes does not include OT-specific risk questions, meaning that 45 changes involving an aviation OT system (air traffic control) were assessed without evaluating OT-specific risks such as control system availability impact, protocol changes, or interaction with safety instrumented systems. An OT change that increases network latency or alters protocol behaviour can have operational safety consequences that are invisible to an IT-focused CIA. The gaps are: (1) emergency changes bypassing CIA with retroactive records only, (2) CIA template not fit for purpose for OT systems, (3) operations director approval used as a substitute for cybersecurity process.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 requires all changes to CII systems to undergo a change management process including cybersecurity impact assessment
Emergency changes may have an expedited path but cannot bypass cybersecurity impact assessment entirely
OT systems require OT-specific cybersecurity impact assessment criteria that standard IT CIA templates do not cover
Retroactive change documentation 2 weeks after the fact does not satisfy the CIA requirement — CIA must be prospective or concurrent
Non-cybersecurity manager approval (operations director) does not substitute for the cybersecurity impact assessment process

reasoning_chain: Review the emergency changes against the CIA requirement — identify that no CIA was conducted
Assess whether retroactive documentation 2 weeks later satisfies the requirement — it does not
Identify the operations director approval as a governance gap (wrong role approving exceptions)
Review the CIA template against OT requirements — identify that OT-specific risks are not assessed

input.question: A water utility CII organization's policy states that system hardening must be applied to all CII servers and network devices using an approved hardening baseline. The IT team confirms that hardening baselines based on CIS Benchmarks are applied to all new server builds. The Risk Manager reviews the hardening compliance records and finds: (a) 12 servers provisioned in the last year have hardening applied at build time; (b) 8 servers provisioned 3 years ago have never had their hardening configuration validated since initial deployment; (c) 6 network devices (switches, routers) in the OT network segment have no hardening baseline applied — the OT team states these were inherited when the CII designation was extended to include the water treatment plant 18 months ago; (d) the hardening baseline has not been updated in 2 years and does not reflect the vendor's current security configuration recommendations. Identify the compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: Four compliance gaps are present in the hardening programme. First, the 8 older servers: applying hardening at build time does not satisfy CCoP requirements on an ongoing basis. Hardening configurations drift over time due to operational changes, patches, and manual interventions. CCoP requires periodic validation of hardening compliance — the 8 servers with no validation since initial deployment (3+ years) are not demonstrably compliant. Second, the 6 OT network devices: inheriting devices as part of a CII boundary extension 18 months ago does not exempt them from hardening requirements. CCoP applies to all assets within the CII digital boundary, and these devices should have been hardened (or assessed for hardening feasibility with compensating controls) within a reasonable period of the boundary extension. 18 months without hardening or documented exception is a compliance gap. Third, the hardening baseline currency: a 2-year-old baseline that does not reflect current vendor security recommendations may contain outdated configurations that fail to address newer vulnerabilities. CCoP requires that hardening standards be kept current. Fourth, there is a policy-practice gap: the policy states hardening is applied to all CII servers and network devices; the OT network devices are excluded in practice. Gaps: (1) no periodic validation of hardening on older servers, (2) OT network devices unhardened 18 months after CII boundary extension, (3) stale hardening baseline, (4) policy-practice inconsistency for OT devices.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 requires system hardening to be applied to all CII systems and validated on an ongoing basis, not only at build time
All assets within the CII digital boundary must meet hardening requirements regardless of when they were inherited into the boundary
Hardening baselines must be kept current and reflect vendor security configuration recommendations
A 2-year gap between hardening baseline updates means newer vulnerabilities may not be addressed by the current configuration standard
CII boundary extensions require systematic compliance review of inherited assets within a reasonable period

reasoning_chain: Identify that hardening at build time is necessary but not sufficient — ongoing validation is required
Review the 8 unvalidated servers against periodic hardening compliance requirement

Assess the hardening baseline currency — 2-year-old baseline is likely stale against current vendor recommendations
Identify the policy-practice gap: policy covers all devices; OT devices are excluded in practice
Characterize and rank the 4 gaps by severity and remediation effort

May recommend a hardening compliance scanning schedule for ongoing validation
May identify the CII boundary extension as a trigger that should have initiated a compliance gap assessment for inherited assets

CII boundary extensions do not require immediate hardening of inherited assets

Attributing specific hardening validation frequency requirements that CCoP does not specify

input.question: A government ministry CII organization's policy states that cybersecurity logs from CII systems must be centrally collected, retained for a minimum period, and reviewed by the security operations team. The Risk Manager reviews the logging infrastructure and finds: (a) enterprise IT systems forward logs to a SIEM with 12 months retention; (b) 4 OT network monitoring sensors in the ministry's smart building management system generate logs that are stored locally on each sensor with 30-day retention, not forwarded to the SIEM; (c) the SIEM receives logs but the security operations team conducts manual log review once per week for anomalies — no automated alerting is configured; (d) the ministry's security policy states logs must be retained for a minimum of 2 years. Identify the compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: Three compliance gaps exist in this logging programme. First, the OT sensor log gap: the 4 smart building management sensors store logs locally with 30-day retention and do not forward to the SIEM. This creates two sub-gaps: (a) the logs are not centrally collected as required by policy and CCoP Section 6, and (b) 30-day local retention is far below the 2-year minimum in the organization's own policy and CCoP requirements. Local-only storage also means the logs are vulnerable to being overwritten or unavailable during an incident investigation. Second, the retention gap on IT systems: the enterprise IT systems have 12 months retention in the SIEM, while the organization's policy mandates 2 years. This is a direct policy-practice gap — the SIEM configuration does not match the retention requirement in the policy. Third, the monitoring effectiveness gap: weekly manual log review without automated alerting means the security operations capability is insufficient for effective threat detection. CCoP Section 6 requires active monitoring and detection capabilities, not just log collection. Adversarial activity can go undetected for a week in the absence of automated alerting. The gaps are: (1) OT sensors not forwarding logs to SIEM, (2) OT sensor retention at 30 days vs 2-year requirement, (3) IT SIEM retention at 12 months vs 2-year requirement, (4) monitoring programme relies on weekly manual review with no automated alerting.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 6 requires that security logs from CII systems be centrally collected and retained
CCoP 2.0 requires that log retention meets defined minimum periods — local short-term retention on individual devices does not satisfy this requirement
CCoP 2.0 requires active monitoring and detection capabilities — log collection alone without timely review is insufficient
A policy-practice gap exists when the SIEM retention (12 months) is less than the policy-mandated minimum (2 years)
OT system logs (including building management, ICS sensors) within the CII boundary must meet the same logging and retention requirements as IT systems

reasoning_chain: Review the logging infrastructure against CCoP Section 6 requirements for central collection and retention
Identify OT sensors as CII-adjacent assets whose logs are not centrally collected — gap 1
Compare OT sensor retention (30 days) against 2-year policy requirement — gap 2 (severity: high)
Compare IT SIEM retention (12 months) against 2-year policy requirement — gap 3 (policy-practice)
Assess monitoring effectiveness: weekly manual review — insufficient for threat detection — gap 4
Rank by severity: OT non-collection > retention gaps > monitoring effectiveness

May recommend syslog forwarding from OT sensors to SIEM or a dedicated OT monitoring solution
May note that the monitoring gap may require investment in a SOC or managed SIEM service

Weekly manual log review is sufficient for CCoP Section 6 monitoring requirements

Attributing GDPR data retention requirements as CCoP logging mandates

input.question: An energy sector CII organization's cybersecurity governance policy states that the board of directors must receive a cybersecurity risk report at least quarterly. The Risk Manager reviews the last 12 months of board meeting minutes and finds: (a) Q1: cybersecurity was a standing agenda item and a full risk report was presented; (b) Q2: the cybersecurity risk item was deferred due to time constraints — a brief verbal update was given with no written report; (c) Q3: no board meeting was held (extraordinary board meeting had been held for a different matter); (d) Q4: the cybersecurity risk report was included in board papers but board minutes show it was not discussed. Additionally, no board member has received formal cybersecurity training in the last 18 months. Identify all governance compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: The governance programme has significant compliance gaps. Regarding board reporting: in Q1 the requirement was met. In Q2, deferral to a verbal briefing without written report does not satisfy the policy requirement for a quarterly report — the absence of a written risk report is both a policy-practice gap and a documentation gap for audit purposes. In Q3, no regular board meeting being held means the quarterly reporting cadence was broken — even if an extraordinary meeting occurred for another purpose, the organization should have either added cybersecurity to the extraordinary meeting agenda or convened an interim update. In Q4, the risk report was distributed but not discussed — a report presented to the board that was not discussed cannot be said to have fulfilled the governance oversight function. Board oversight requires engagement, not just distribution. On board training: no board member has received cybersecurity training in 18 months. CCoP 2.0 Section 3 requires at least one board member to have cybersecurity knowledge and awareness, and this expectation will be reinforced by the 2026 regulatory changes mandating board training. 18 months without any training is a governance gap. The aggregate picture shows a governance programme that exists on paper but has not delivered meaningful board oversight for 3 of the last 4 quarters. Gaps: (1) Q2 verbal briefing not satisfying written report requirement, (2) Q3 reporting gap, (3) Q4 undiscussed report, (4) board member training 18 months lapsed.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 3 requires board-level cybersecurity oversight including regular reporting on cybersecurity risk posture
A written cybersecurity risk report presented to the board is a required audit artefact — verbal briefings do not substitute
Board members must have cybersecurity knowledge and awareness under CCoP 2.0 governance requirements
A risk report distributed to the board but not discussed does not demonstrate meaningful board oversight of cybersecurity risk
The upcoming 2026 regulatory requirement for mandatory board cybersecurity training will formalize what is already an implicit CCoP 2.0 expectation

reasoning_chain: Review the 4 quarters of board meeting minutes against the quarterly reporting requirement
Q1: compliant; Q2: verbal briefing insufficient; Q3: reporting gap; Q4: distributed but not discussed
Identify each non-compliant quarter and characterize the nature of the gap
Assess board training gap — 18 months without training violates CCoP governance requirements
Characterize the aggregate picture: governance programme exists on paper but has not delivered meaningful oversight
Rank gaps: undiscussed Q4 report = high (most subtle, hardest to remediate); Q2 verbal = medium; Q3 gap = high; training = high
acceptable_variations: May recommend a standing cybersecurity board committee to ensure consistent agenda time
May recommend a board-level cybersecurity KPI dashboard to support engagement
May note that the 2026 board training requirement makes immediate action on training particularly important

A verbal briefing at a board meeting fulfills the written quarterly report requirement
hallucination_patterns: Citing a specific number of board members required to have cybersecurity qualifications
Attributing specific board cybersecurity training hours from a non-CCoP source

input.question: A healthcare CII organization has completed a business continuity and disaster recovery (BCP/DR) planning exercise. The CISO presents the following BCP/DR documentation to the Risk Manager for review: (a) a BCP document last updated 2 years ago; (b) a DR plan last tested 20 months ago — the test was a tabletop exercise that did not include actual failover to the DR site; (c) the BCP does not address the scenario of a ransomware attack on the hospital's patient data systems, which is the most common threat scenario identified in the current threat model; (d) no DR plan exists for the hospital's building management system (HVAC, access control, nurse call systems) which were added to the CII boundary extension 10 months ago. Identify the compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: Four compliance gaps are present in the BCP/DR programme. First, BCP currency: the BCP is 2 years old and has not been updated to reflect current threat scenarios, particularly ransomware. CCoP 2.0 requires BCP/DR documents to be maintained and updated to remain relevant to the current threat landscape. A BCP that does not address the organization's most significant identified threat (ransomware) is not fit for purpose. Second, DR test adequacy: a tabletop exercise that did not include actual failover does not demonstrate that the DR capability will function under real conditions. CCoP requires periodic testing of the DR capability, including technical failover testing, not only tabletop discussions. Third, the building management system coverage gap: the HVAC, access control, and nurse call systems were added to the CII boundary 10 months ago and have no DR plan. For a healthcare CII, loss of HVAC can affect medical equipment and patient safety; loss of access control affects physical security. These are critical operational systems requiring DR coverage. Fourth, no full-scale test: the last DR test was 20 months ago (overdue if the test cycle is annual), and the test format (tabletop only) was insufficient. The combination means the organization does not have recent evidence that its DR capability works. Gaps: (1) BCP outdated and missing ransomware scenario, (2) DR test methodology insufficient (no actual failover), (3) no DR plan for building management systems in CII boundary, (4) DR test cycle lapsed.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 8 requires BCP and DR plans to be maintained, relevant to current threats, and regularly tested
DR testing must include technical failover testing — tabletop exercises alone do not demonstrate operational DR capability
All systems within the CII digital boundary, including newly added systems, must be covered by BCP/DR plans
BCP must address current threat scenarios identified in the organization's threat model — a BCP that ignores the primary identified threat is not fit for purpose
Building management systems (HVAC, access control) in a healthcare CII context have patient safety implications if unavailable — DR priority is higher than typical IT systems

reasoning_chain: Assess BCP currency — 2 years old with no ransomware scenario, the primary identified threat
Map the ransomware gap against CCoP requirement for BCP to reflect current threat landscape
Assess DR test adequacy — tabletop without failover does not demonstrate DR capability
Identify the building management systems as a DR coverage gap following CII boundary extension
Assess DR test timing — 20 months potentially overdue if annual test cycle applies
Characterize 4 gaps in order of severity: ransomware scenario gap (highest), DR test methodology, no DR for OT/building systems, test cycle lapsed

May recommend failover testing to a cold standby site using non-production systems first
May note the patient safety implications of building management system failure in healthcare

BCP plans do not need to address specific threat scenarios — a generic plan is sufficient

Attributing healthcare-specific BCP requirements from MOH guidelines as CCoP mandates

input.question: A maritime CII organization's documented cybersecurity policy states that network segmentation must separate OT systems from IT systems and from the internet, using a layered defence approach. The organization's actual network architecture review shows: (a) the vessel traffic management (VTM) system is on a dedicated OT network segment separated from the corporate IT network by a firewall; (b) the firewall rules allow bi-directional traffic between the corporate network and the VTM OT segment on port 3389 (Remote Desktop Protocol) to allow IT support staff to assist VTM operators; (c) there is no DMZ between the corporate IT network and the OT segment — the firewall directly connects both segments; (d) the corporate IT network is connected to the internet via a perimeter firewall. Identify the network segmentation compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: The network architecture has significant segmentation gaps relative to both the organization's policy and CCoP 2.0 requirements. First, the RDP access gap: bi-directional traffic on RDP (port 3389) between corporate IT and the VTM OT segment fundamentally undermines network segmentation. RDP is a high-value lateral movement vector — it was used in the vast majority of significant ICS attacks. Allowing RDP directly into the OT segment means any compromise of a corporate IT workstation can lead to direct access to the VTM system. This violates the defence-in-depth and layered defence principles mandated in CCoP 2.0 and is a policy-practice gap (policy says layered defence; architecture has direct OT access via RDP). Second, the missing DMZ: CCoP 2.0 OT Addendum requires a DMZ architecture between IT and OT networks. The direct firewall connection without a DMZ means there is no intermediate inspection zone, no bastion host requirement, and no data diode option for unidirectional data flows. Third, these two gaps are compounded: RDP into the OT segment without a DMZ means IT staff can access the OT network using high-risk protocol from a network connected to the internet, with no additional inspection layer. For a vessel traffic management system, this represents a critical safety-security risk. Gaps: (1) bi-directional RDP access into OT segment violating layered defence policy, (2) missing DMZ between IT and OT networks, (3) RDP without DMZ creates a direct internet-to-OT access path via corporate IT compromise.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 OT Addendum requires a DMZ architecture between IT and OT networks to implement layered defence
RDP (port 3389) is a high-risk lateral movement vector — allowing bi-directional RDP from corporate IT into OT networks violates CCoP network segmentation requirements
CCoP 2.0 requires defence-in-depth and layered defence architecture for CII networks — direct firewall connection between IT and OT without DMZ does not satisfy this requirement
A policy-practice gap exists between the documented policy (layered defence) and the actual architecture (no DMZ, direct RDP access)
For vessel traffic management systems, a successful attack via OT network access can have navigational safety consequences beyond cybersecurity impact

reasoning_chain: Review the network architecture against the layered defence policy and CCoP OT Addendum requirements
Identify RDP bi-directional access as a high-risk protocol violation in the OT segmentation design
Identify the missing DMZ as a structural architecture gap
Connect the two gaps: RDP without DMZ creates a compounded internet-to-OT access risk
Identify the policy-practice gap between documented layered defence policy and actual direct-connection architecture
Characterize the combined security risk for a vessel traffic management system
acceptable_variations: May recommend replacing RDP with a jump server in a DMZ with session recording
May recommend data diodes for one-way data flows from OT to IT where bi-directional access is not operationally required
May note that firewall rules alone do not constitute the DMZ architecture required by the OT Addendum

forbidden_claims: A firewall between IT and OT segments satisfies the DMZ requirement in the CCoP OT Addendum
RDP access to OT systems is acceptable if restricted to IT support staff
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific firewall rule requirements from CCoP that it does not specify
Attributing IEC 62443 zone and conduit requirements as CCoP mandates

input.question: A banking CII organization's supply chain policy states that all third-party vendors with access to CII systems must undergo a cybersecurity risk assessment before access is granted and annually thereafter. The Risk Manager audits the vendor risk management programme and finds: (a) the 5 primary vendors (core banking system provider, payment gateway operator, network monitoring vendor, backup services vendor, and security testing firm) all have completed initial assessments and annual re-assessments; (b) 12 sub-vendors used by the core banking system provider have access to the CII during maintenance activities — none have been assessed; (c) the payment gateway operator had a significant security incident reported by MAS 6 months ago — the annual re-assessment for this vendor is not due for another 3 months; (d) the security testing firm's assessment is based entirely on the firm's self-attestation questionnaire with no independent verification. Identify all supply chain compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: The supply chain programme has gaps at sub-vendor, incident-triggered review, and assessment quality levels. First, sub-vendor gap: the 12 sub-vendors of the core banking system provider have maintenance access to the CII but have not been assessed. CCoP 2.0 requires that the organization manages cybersecurity risk across its supply chain — including sub-vendors who have access to CII. The core banking vendor's use of unassessed sub-contractors with CII access is a compliance gap, regardless of whether the prime vendor has been assessed. Second, incident-triggered review: the payment gateway vendor experienced a significant security incident 6 months ago reported to MAS. CCoP does not limit risk assessments to scheduled annual cycles — a material security incident at a vendor with CII access is an event that triggers an immediate risk review, not a wait-until-scheduled approach. The 3-month delay represents an unacceptable risk acceptance period for a vendor whose security posture is known to have deteriorated. Third, assessment quality: relying entirely on vendor self-attestation for the security testing firm's assessment is insufficient. Independent verification of material security claims is a requirement for meaningful vendor risk management. A security testing firm with unverified access to CII is a high-risk assessment gap. Gaps: (1) sub-vendors with CII access not assessed, (2) no incident-triggered review of payment gateway vendor, (3) self-attestation-only assessment for security testing firm.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 supply chain requirements extend to sub-vendors who have access to CII systems — the prime vendor's assessment does not cover sub-contractors
A material security incident at a vendor with CII access triggers an immediate risk review — the annual cycle does not apply when a known security event has occurred
Vendor risk assessments based solely on self-attestation without independent verification are insufficient for CCoP supply chain compliance
Security testing firms with access to CII require particularly rigorous assessment given their privileged access during test activities
MAS-reported security incidents at vendors are material events that CIIOs must factor into their own risk assessments

reasoning_chain: Review the vendor programme against CCoP supply chain requirements
Identify the 12 sub-vendors as having CII access without any assessment — gap 1
Identify the payment gateway incident as a material event triggering immediate review — gap 2
Assess the security testing firm assessment quality: self-attestation only — gap 3
Note the heightened risk of security testing firm access (they know the attack surface)
Characterize gaps: sub-vendor coverage, incident-triggered review, assessment quality
acceptable_variations: May recommend flow-down of cybersecurity requirements to sub-vendors via prime vendor contracts
May recommend an interim risk review of the payment gateway vendor without waiting for the annual cycle
May suggest independent audit or penetration test verification for security testing firm assessments

forbidden_claims: Sub-vendors who access CII through an assessed prime vendor do not require separate assessment
Annual re-assessment cycles take precedence over incident-triggered reviews
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific vendor assessment questionnaire requirements from CCoP
Attributing MAS-TRM vendor risk management requirements as CCoP mandates

input.question: An energy sector CII organization's policy states that cryptography must be used to protect sensitive data in transit and at rest for all CII systems. The Risk Manager reviews the cryptography implementation and finds: (a) all external-facing web services use TLS 1.2 or higher; (b) internal communications between CII application servers use TLS 1.0 — the application team states upgrading to TLS 1.2 would require application changes; (c) data at rest on CII database servers is encrypted using AES-128; (d) backup tapes containing CII data are transported off-site by a courier without encryption — the backup system creates unencrypted tape images; (e) communications between the SCADA master station and remote terminal units use a legacy proprietary protocol with no encryption or authentication. Identify the compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: Multiple cryptography compliance gaps are present. First, TLS 1.0 on internal communications: TLS 1.0 has known vulnerabilities (POODLE, BEAST) and has been deprecated by IETF. CCoP 2.0 requires use of current, approved cryptographic algorithms — TLS 1.0 does not meet this standard. The application change requirement is an operational cost, not a compliance exception. This is a gap requiring a remediation plan. Second, unencrypted backup tapes in transit: off-site backup tapes containing CII data transported by courier without encryption is a significant gap. Data in transit must be protected using encryption — physical transport via courier does not exempt data from the encryption requirement. A single lost or stolen tape exposes CII data without any cryptographic protection. Third, the SCADA RTU communication protocol: legacy proprietary protocols with no encryption or authentication are common in OT environments but represent a compliance gap under CCoP 2.0 OT Addendum requirements for secure communications. This gap is recognized as operationally complex — the appropriate path is a waiver with compensating controls (physical security of field devices, network monitoring for abnormal SCADA commands) or a technology refresh roadmap. Note that AES-128 for data at rest is borderline — while not prohibited, current best practice recommends AES-256 for sensitive data. The gaps are: (1) deprecated TLS 1.0 for internal communications, (2) unencrypted backup tapes in physical transit, (3) no encryption/authentication on SCADA-RTU communications.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 requires use of approved and current cryptographic algorithms — TLS 1.0 is deprecated and does not satisfy this requirement
Data in transit must be encrypted regardless of the transport medium — physical courier transport of unencrypted backup tapes containing CII data is a compliance gap
SCADA-RTU communications without encryption or authentication are an OT security gap requiring either compensating controls with waiver or technology refresh roadmap
Application change requirements are operational costs, not compliance exceptions — deprecated protocols require remediation plans
Physical transport of storage media containing CII data requires the same cryptographic protections as electronic transmission

reasoning_chain: Assess each communication and storage element against CCoP cryptography requirements
Identify TLS 1.0 as deprecated — application change cost does not exempt it
Identify unencrypted physical tape transport as a data-in-transit encryption gap
Identify SCADA-RTU protocol as an OT encryption gap — recognize operational complexity
Note AES-128 as borderline but not a hard gap
Characterize gaps: deprecated TLS (application gap), unencrypted tape transport (data gap), SCADA protocol (OT gap requiring waiver pathway)
acceptable_variations: May recommend tape encryption at the backup software level rather than hardware upgrade
May recommend data diode or encrypted gateway between SCADA and RTUs as a compensating control
May note that a waiver is likely appropriate for the SCADA-RTU protocol gap given operational constraints

forbidden_claims: TLS 1.0 is acceptable for internal communications if external communications use TLS 1.2
Physical courier transport of backup tapes is not subject to the data-in-transit encryption requirement
hallucination_patterns: Citing specific algorithm deprecation dates from a non-CCoP standard as CCoP requirements
Attributing FIPS 140-2 cryptography standards as CCoP mandates

input.question: A transport sector CII organization's cybersecurity policy states that all CII systems must be included in the cybersecurity exercise programme, with at least one full-scale exercise per year. The Risk Manager reviews the exercise programme for the past year and finds: (a) a tabletop exercise was conducted in March involving the IT and cybersecurity teams; (b) a red team exercise was conducted in July — the scope was limited to enterprise IT systems, explicitly excluding the rail signalling and ticketing systems; (c) the annual full-scale exercise scheduled for November was cancelled due to operational constraints and was not rescheduled; (d) no CSA notification of exercises was given; (e) the after-action report from the March tabletop identified 8 improvement actions, of which 5 remain open. Identify all exercise programme compliance gaps.

ground_truth.expected_response: The exercise programme has significant compliance gaps across scope, format, and follow-through dimensions. First, the annual full-scale exercise was cancelled and not rescheduled — this means the organization did not conduct a full-scale exercise as required by its policy and CCoP 2.0 Section 9. Operational constraints cannot unilaterally excuse non-performance of a mandatory annual exercise. The appropriate response was rescheduling or seeking CSA guidance on deferrals. Second, the red team exercise scope explicitly excluded the rail signalling and ticketing systems — which are the core CII components. An exercise programme that deliberately excludes CII systems does not test the most material aspects of the organization's cybersecurity resilience. CCoP requires that exercises cover CII systems, not just enterprise IT. Third, the 5 open improvement actions from the March tabletop: leaving 5 of 8 improvement actions unresolved represents a failure to learn from exercises, which is the primary purpose of the exercise programme under CCoP Section 9. Fourth, CSA must be notified of CII cybersecurity exercises — no notification was given. This is a procedural compliance gap. Fifth, the March tabletop included only IT and cybersecurity teams — OT operations teams were excluded. For a transport CII, signalling system operators and operations managers are critical exercise participants. The gaps are: (1) no full-scale exercise conducted, (2) CII systems excluded from red team scope, (3) open improvement actions, (4) CSA notification not given, (5) OT/operations excluded from tabletop.

key_facts.fact: CCoP 2.0 Section 9 requires CII organizations to conduct regular cybersecurity exercises covering their CII systems
CSA must be notified of CII cybersecurity exercises — failure to notify is a procedural compliance gap
Red team and penetration test exercises must cover CII systems — explicitly scoping out CII systems defeats the purpose of the exercise requirement
Exercise improvement actions must be tracked to closure — open actions represent unaddressed resilience weaknesses
OT and operations teams must be included in exercises for CII organizations with OT components — IT-only exercises do not test OT incident response capability

reasoning_chain: Assess the exercise programme against the annual full-scale exercise requirement — cancelled, not rescheduled: gap
Review the red team scope — CII systems explicitly excluded: gap
Review improvement action tracking — 5/8 open: gap
Identify CSA notification requirement — not satisfied: gap
Assess exercise participant coverage — OT/operations not included: gap
Characterize 5 gaps: (1) no full-scale exercise, (2) CII excluded from red team, (3) open improvement actions, (4) CSA notification, (5) OT team excluded
acceptable_variations: May distinguish between the cancelled full-scale exercise and partial exercises as different severities of gap
May recommend a combined IT/OT tabletop as an interim measure before the next red team exercise
May note that CSA may accept a retrospective notification if proactively disclosed

CSA notification of exercises is a recommendation, not a mandatory requirement

Attributing red team methodology standards from CBEST or TIBER as CCoP requirements

input.question: A telecoms CII organization's policy states that threat intelligence must be collected, analyzed, and operationalized to improve detection and prevention controls. The cybersecurity team's threat intelligence programme consists of: (a) subscription to a commercial threat intelligence feed which generates 200-400 indicators of compromise (IoCs) daily; (b) the IoCs are ingested into the SIEM and used for alerting; (c) no strategic or operational threat intelligence is produced — the team only consumes tactical IoCs; (d) the threat intelligence is not shared with CSA or sector peers under the cybersecurity information sharing programme; (e) the last threat intelligence review meeting was 8 months ago. Identify any compliance gaps in the threat intelligence programme.

ground_truth.expected_response: The threat intelligence programme has gaps in both depth and information sharing obligations. First, the programme scope is limited to tactical IoC consumption — there is no strategic or operational threat intelligence capability. CCoP 2.0 Section 6 requires a threat intelligence programme that goes beyond tactical IoC feeds to include understanding of the threat actor landscape targeting Singapore CII and sector-specific threats. A telecoms CII organization faces sophisticated, persistent adversaries — tactical IoCs are necessary but not sufficient. Second, the information sharing gap is a direct CCoP compliance issue. CCoP 2.0 requires CIIOs to participate in cyber threat intelligence sharing with CSA and sector peers. The organization is only consuming threat intelligence and not contributing to the shared ecosystem. Non-participation in threat intelligence sharing is a specific compliance obligation, not a recommendation. Third, 8 months since the last threat intelligence review meeting suggests the programme is not being actively managed or integrated into security decision-making. Fourth, IoC-only tactical intelligence does not feed threat modelling updates, which require strategic threat actor intelligence. This creates a downstream gap in threat model currency. ground_truth.expected_response: Multiple access management gaps exist across access review timeliness, dormant account remediation, and contractor coverage. Either they were excluded from the review scope (a process gap) or they were not provisioned through the standard provisioning process (an access management gap). Contractors with privileged access must be included in access reviews. Fourth, the Q3 delay (3 weeks late) while minor compared to Q4, represents a pattern of deteriorating access review discipline. input.question: A water utility CII organization states in its policy that cyber threat intelligence is shared with CSA and sector peers and that threat hunting activities are conducted proactively. ground_truth.expected_response: The threat hunting programme is not compliant with CCoP 2.0 Section 6 requirements across capability, frequency, documentation, and sharing dimensions. First, capability gap: threat hunting performed ad hoc by the incident response team when capacity allows is not a threat hunting programme — it is occasional investigative activity. Second, frequency gap: 3 hunts in 12 months with a 5-month gap since July suggests the programme is irregular. For a water utility CII — whose OT systems are safety-critical and an attractive target for state-sponsored actors — more frequent threat hunting is expected. The lack of hunts in the second half of the year also means no coverage during a period that historically sees elevated cyber threat activity. Third, documentation gap: informal team chat logs are not audit-ready documentation. CCoP requires that threat hunting activities produce formal records that can be presented as audit evidence. The organization cannot demonstrate what was hunted, what was found, and how findings were addressed. Fourth, sharing gap: hunt findings have never been shared with CSA or sector peers, violating the information sharing requirement. Threat hunting findings are exactly the type of intelligence that sector sharing programmes are designed to distribute. input.question: A banking CII organization's active directory (AD) security is reviewed by the Risk Manager as part of audit preparation. The AD environment covers the CII core banking applications. The review finds: (a) the AD forest and domain functional level is Windows Server 2012 R2 (not current); (b) no Protected Users security group is in use; (c) Kerberos delegation is configured as unconstrained for 3 service accounts that access the core banking application servers; (d) 2 domain controller servers have not received Windows security updates in 6 months; (e) there is no tiering model separating tier-0 assets (domain controllers) from tier-1 (servers) and tier-2 (workstations). Identify the compliance gaps in the AD environment.

ground_truth.expected_response: The Active Directory environment has multiple compliance gaps under CCoP 2.0 requirements for access control and system hardening. First, the outdated functional level: Windows Server 2012 R2 functional level is end-of-life and lacks modern security features including credential protection improvements in WS2016+. Running CII on end-of-life platform components is a hardening and patch management gap. Second, no Protected Users group: CCoP 2.0 specifically references Active Directory security controls including Protected Users security group implementation for privileged accounts on CII. This is a named control — its absence is a compliance gap. Third, unconstrained Kerberos delegation for service accounts: unconstrained Kerberos delegation allows those service accounts to impersonate any user, including domain administrators. This is a critical access control vulnerability for CII — if any of the 3 service accounts is compromised, an attacker gains domain administrator equivalent access. CCoP requires least-privilege configuration of service accounts. Fourth, 6-month unpatched domain controllers: domain controllers are tier-0 assets — the most privileged systems in the AD environment. 6-month patch gap on tier-0 assets is a critical compliance gap. Fifth, no AD tiering model: CCoP 2.0 explicitly references AD tiering as a required control for CII. The absence of tiering means administrative credentials can pass freely between tiers, enabling lateral movement from workstations to domain controllers. Gaps: (1) outdated functional level, (2) no Protected Users group, (3) unconstrained Kerberos delegation, (4) unpatched domain controllers, (5) no tiering model.
